Question nine. How do you join two datasets in memory without a database? Build a dict from the smaller side, keyed on the join column: user ID to name. Then scan the larger side, and look up each order's user. That's a hash join, order n plus m. Comparing every order with every user is order n times m. The follow-up: an order whose user isn't there. Square brackets raise a key error. Get returns none and keeps the order, as a left join would. Writing it out has its own pattern.

Question ten. How do you split a large stream into fixed-size batches? An insert per row pays a round trip per row. A million rows in batches of a thousand is a thousand calls. Pull n items at a time from the iterator with i-slice, until a pull comes back empty. Seven items in threes: three, three, and a last batch of one. Since Python three twelve, itertools batched does exactly this. And when a call fails, you retry it, carefully.

Question eleven. How do you make a network call resilient with retries and backoff? Catch transient errors, wait, and try again, doubling the wait each time. Here the call fails twice, waits ten milliseconds, then twenty, and succeeds on the third try. Then add jitter. Model six clients failing in one outage: with plain backoff, they all come back together, at one, three, seven and fifteen seconds. Wait a random time up to each delay instead, and their retries spread out. Know what not to retry, too. A bad request fails the same way every time, so it's raised at once. Cap the attempts, and retry only what's safe to repeat: a retried payment can charge twice. Safe to repeat has a name.
